# Deep Dive — Browser & Android Automation, Web Scraping, Data Extraction, and Raw→Structured Data

**Companion to:** `oss-categories-report-2026-09.md` (the 65-category report). This document expands the categories the user flagged for deeper coverage — browser automation, Android emulator/device control, and the adjacent pipeline of web scraping → data extraction → raw data converted into structured data — into seven sub-groups with landscape notes and full-row metadata.

**Scope.** Same two source documents (`listings/index.html` — 7,268 GitHub repo entries distilled from 385 YouTube showcase videos; `listings/products_viewer_unified.html` — 11,226 Product Hunt products, Jun–Sep 2026). Where the listings are thin (most visibly: **Android device/emulator tooling, and the classic foundation libraries of scraping and data processing**), canonical tools were added as clearly-marked **＋ web gap-fill** rows, confirmed against 2026 comparison sources via the research toolkit's free DDG engine and health-verified live. No other files from the repo-showcase tree were consulted beyond the permitted README folder.

**Method.** Candidate pools came from the keyword categories `browser-control`, `web-scraping`, `data-conversion`, `text-extract` and adjacent buckets of the main run; picks were then hand-grouped into the seven sub-groups below (a tool can conceptually belong to two groups — e.g. vercel-labs/agent-browser, PaddleOCR — it is listed once, in its most-load-bearing group). Every repo, listing-sourced or gap-fill, was verified via `gh api repos/OWNER/REPO` on **2026-09-22**; ★ shows `listing→GH` where the numbers drifted.

**As of 2026-09-22. Toolkit spend: $0 (free DDG engine only; Tavily allowance untouched).**

---

## Summary of findings

1. **The agent-browser layer has fully arrived.** browser-use (★88k at listing capture, ★116k today), the Chrome/Playwright MCP bridges, Stagehand and Skyvern are all top-of-listing, actively-pushed, and mutually complementary rather than competing — the 2026 stack has standardized on Playwright underneath with LLM drivers above it.
2. **Android is the listings' blind spot.** 3 tools across 385 videos vs. a canonical ecosystem (scrcpy ★150k, Appium, Detox, Airtest, STF, redroid) that never appears. The gap-fill table is the recommendation.
3. **Scraping has four coexisting generations** (classic frameworks → LLM-native crawlers → no-code robots → specialists), and the classics are not dead: Scrapy and trafilatura are both pushed this week.
4. **Document extraction is the most crowded space in the entire source corpus** — 20+ actively-pushed projects in the listings alone, converging on PDF→Markdown-for-LLMs with OCR foundation models underneath.
5. **The structuring layer's foundations were also absent from the listings** (pandas, polars, SheetJS, csvkit, readability, pdfplumber) despite every layer above depending on them.

## Browser Automation — Frameworks, SDKs & Infrastructure

This is the foundation layer everything else in the document builds on. Puppeteer (Chrome DevTools protocol direct) and Playwright (multi-browser, multi-language, auto-waiting) remain the two canonical SDKs; the listings captured both at high star counts with only modest drift since capture, confirming they are still the default picks in 2026. SeleniumBase carries the Selenium-lineage flag for Python with batteries included (UC mode doubles as light anti-detect). Below the SDKs sits infrastructure: browserless runs headless browsers as a service, Lightpanda (Zig) and obscura (Rust) are the new lightweight-headless-engine contenders purpose-built for scraping/agent workloads where a full Chromium is too heavy, and Crawlee (TypeScript + Python) wraps the SDKs into a crawling framework with queueing, retries and proxy rotation. At the long tail, helium wraps Selenium in a much simpler API, ferret offers a declarative query language for web scraping, and pinchtab is a Go browser-automation bridge/orchestrator aimed at running many instances with stealth defaults. Vercel's agent-browser (Rust CLI, no Node runtime) appears in section 2 conceptually but is listed here since it is at heart a framework CLI.

## AI-Agent-Driven Browser Control & MCP Bridges

The fastest-moving layer of the whole landscape, and the listings cover it well. browser-use (Python) is the de-facto standard LLM browser driver and the hub of an ecosystem (web-ui for a local GUI, browser-harness for self-healing selectors). Stagehand (browserbase) takes the opposite approach — deterministic Playwright code with AI only at the edges (its `act`/`extract`/`observe` primitives) — which is where most production teams have landed. Skyvern targets visual, DOM-optional workflow automation; Open-AutoGLM extends the pattern to phone screens (bridge to section 4). The MCP bridges (chrome-devtools-mcp, playwright-mcp, mcp-playwright) let coding agents drive a real browser over the Model Context Protocol and are now among the most-installed MCP servers overall. BrowserOS is the full Chromium-fork answer: a browser whose entire UI is agent-first. A 2026 selection rule of thumb that falls out of the metadata: use browser-use for agent autonomy, Stagehand for controllability, an MCP bridge when the consumer is a coding agent, and raw Playwright when neither the LLM nor the autonomy is actually needed.

## Stealth / Anti-Detect Browsers & Evasion Patches

Anti-bot evasion splits into three implementation strategies, all present here. Camoufox is a custom Firefox build with fingerprint spoofing at the C++ level, driven through Playwright — the deep-patching approach. CloakBrowser ships a stealth Chromium as a drop-in Playwright replacement, and camofox-browser exposes a stealth headless server aimed directly at AI agents; both are newer and more commercial-adjacent. The patch-layer approach is represented by the two gap-fills: patchright (patched Playwright distributions that defeat common headless detection) and rebrowser-patches (the maintained CDP-runtime-leak patches). Choose by how much of the stack you control: patch a stock browser (rebrowser/patchright) when you must stay on Chromium/Playwright, run a hardened build (camoufox/CloakBrowser) when fingerprinting is the problem. Fortress on Product Hunt targets the same need as a commercial anti-detect product. **Legal note:** evasion tooling sits in a grey zone — it is legitimate for testing your own sites and for accessibility, and ToS-violating for most scraping targets; the listings showcase them, this report only verifies the metadata.

## Android & Mobile Device Automation (Emulators, Device Control)

**This is the thinnest category in the source listings relative to how big the ecosystem is — the gap-fill layer below is larger than the listings layer, which is itself the finding.** Only three Android-control tools appear across all 385 showcase videos: escrcpy (a GUI for scrcpy), X-OmniClaw (a ★262 agent-claw experiment), and sim-use (LY Corp's iOS/Android simulator control for agents). Meanwhile the canonical stack — scrcpy at ★150k, one of the most-starred projects on all of GitHub — is absent, as are Appium, Detox, Airtest and uiautomator2. The showcase channels simply don't cover device-farm and emulator tooling; the gap-fill rows are the real recommendation list here. They map the stack top to bottom: mirroring/control (scrcpy, QtScrcpy), UI automation frameworks (Appium cross-platform, Detox for React Native, Airtest for games, uiautomator2 for Python instrumented control), agent-era device control (lamda — an RPA server on top of a modified scrcpy), device farms (STF for real-device labs, redroid for containerized Android-in-Docker at scale, and Google's emulator container scripts for CI). Note on Maestro: it is the other big-name mobile UI test framework, but it has no canonical OSS repository on GitHub (only the ★481 `devicelab-dev/maestro-runner` mirror), so it is excluded from the tables.

## Web Scraping & Crawling

The listings are strong here — this is the best-covered layer of the expansion. The 2026 landscape splits into four generations, all live: classic frameworks (Scrapy — still ★64k and actively pushed; the gap-fill trafilatura for main-content extraction), LLM-native crawlers (crawl4ai, ScrapeGraphAI, gpt-researcher), visual/no-code robots (EasySpider, maxun — "website → API without code"), and recon-flavored specialists (katana for crawling-as-security-tooling, maigret for username enumeration across 3000+ sites, MediaCrawler for social platforms, Agent-Reach for giving agents read/search capabilities over Twitter/Reddit/YouTube). Firecrawl dominates mindshare (★159k at capture, ★183k today — the fastest-growing item in this section) and its spin-offs (pdf-inspector, anydoc) are classified in section 6. Huginn and trendFinder cover monitoring/agents rather than one-shot scraping. jina-ai/reader rounds it out as the URL→LLM-text API. A defensible 2026 default: Scrapy for scale, crawl4ai when the target is LLM ingestion, Scrapling when the sites fight back, EasySpider/maxun when the user is not a programmer.

## Document & Text Extraction (PDF, HTML, OCR)

Document→text is where the listings are densest and most current — the entire modern OCR/document-AI wave is captured. The center of gravity is the "PDF/document → Markdown/JSON for LLMs" cohort: docling (IBM), MinerU and PDF-Extract-Kit (OpenDataLab), marker + chandra (datalab), unstructured, plus the newer specialized engines (kreuzberg — polyglot Rust; liteparse; omniparse; firecrawl's anydoc and pdf-inspector). A second cohort is OCR foundation models, which in 2025–2026 converged on "context compression" architectures: DeepSeek-OCR and DeepSeek-OCR-2, olmocr (Ai2), Dolphin (ByteDance), GLM-OCR, Baidu's Unlimited-OCR. Around the models sit applications: Stirling-PDF and paperless-ngx (self-hosted PDF manipulation and document management), LaTeX-OCR (formula images→LaTeX), opendataloader-pdf (accessibility-focused parsing), and easy-dataset (dataset preparation for fine-tuning). The HTML side is the gap-fill: mozilla/readability is the reader-mode extraction engine inside every major browser and most scraping stacks, html2text its simplest Python ancestor, and pdfplumber/PyMuPDF the two PDF libraries everything above is ultimately built on or compared against. Choosing among the LLM-era parsers is genuinely workload-dependent; the table's topics and language columns are the fastest discriminator.

## Raw Data → Structured Data (Conversion, Pipelines, Structured Outputs)

The last mile: turning extracted text and raw files into validated, queryable structure. markitdown (Microsoft) is the flagship anything→Markdown converter for LLM ingestion. For tabular/analytical structure the DataFrame layer is foundational and was entirely absent from the listings: pandas remains the default (★50k), polars (Rust) is the performance successor (★40k, pushed today), SheetJS dominates the Excel side (note: its GitHub repo has not been pushed since 2024 — development moved off-GitHub after the license change), and csvkit is the classic CSV CLI Swiss army knife. For LLM outputs specifically, instructor (patched clients that force pydantic-validated structured outputs) and outlines (constrained generation) are the two standards. Above them sit the pipeline/orchestration engines captured by the listings: Airflow and Kestra for scheduling, SeaTunnel and redpanda-connect for data integration/streaming, Daft for multimodal DataFrames, pathway and cocoindex for incremental/streaming LLM pipelines, graphrag (Microsoft) for the RAG-specific transformation, and unstract as the no-code LLM-document-platform layer. The Product Hunt rows (HFlow, ETLFunnel CE, MCVT, JSON to Excel) are all small conversion utilities — included for completeness, not as recommendations.

## Addendum — The Foundation Layer: A Deep Dive on the Classics (2026-09-22)

*Follow-up to finding #5 above ("the classics were also absent — Scrapy, trafilatura, readability, pandas, polars, pdfplumber…"). This section deep-dives that foundation layer and the other load-bearing libraries the showcase listings skip, researched via the toolkit's free DDG engine and gh-verified on 2026-09-22. None of these appear in the source listings; every row is a ＋ addition. Where a tool already sits in sections 5–7 above (Scrapy, trafilatura, readability, pdfplumber, PyMuPDF, pandas, polars, csvkit, SheetJS, DuckDB), it is not repeated — this addendum completes the picture around them.*

The one-line verdict up front: **the classics are not legacy — they are the load-bearing infrastructure the entire 2026 wave is built on, and almost all of them are pushed more recently than the showcase tools.** 15 of the 20 repos below were pushed within six weeks of the check date; the five laggards are exactly the ones the 2026 wave has replaced or that simply need no changes — the two dormant anti-bot classics (undetected-chromedriver, cloudscraper), the archived bs4 GitHub mirror, and httpx/pdfminer.six at a mature ~6-month cadence. The YouTube showcase ecosystem skips this layer because it is infrastructure, not because it is dead.

### A. HTTP clients & the classic anti-bot stack

Selenium is the twenty-year patriarch of browser automation (now under the Selenium Foundation-level governance, pushed daily) and remains the W3C WebDriver reference that Appium and friends build on. requests and httpx are the plain-HTTP defaults — httpx when you need async or HTTP/2. The interesting 2026 story is the aging of the classic anti-bot trio: **undetected-chromedriver** (last push 2025-07) and **cloudscraper** (2025-06) have gone quiet for ~15 months, and their role has been absorbed by the section-3 stealth wave (camoufox, CloakBrowser, patchright, rebrowser-patches) for browser-based work and by **curl_cffi** — TLS/JA3/HTTP2 fingerprint impersonation without a browser, pushed the same day as this check — for HTTP-level work. **FlareSolverr** remains the household proxy-style Cloudflare bypass that media-server stacks depend on.

Selenium is an umbrella project for a range of tools and libraries that enable and support the automation of web browsers. Selenium specifically provides an infrastructure for the W3C WebDriver specification — a platform and language-neutral coding interface compatible with all major web browsers. Selenium WebDriver If you want to create robust, browser-based regression automation suites and tests, scale and distribute scripts across many environments, then you want to use Selenium WebDriver, a collection of language specific bindings to drive a browser - the way it is meant to be driven. How it works FlareSolverr starts a proxy server, and it waits for user requests in an idle state using few resources. When some request arrives, it uses Selenium with the undetected-chromedriver to create a web browser (Chrome). I found it while looking for a way to fix a problem: my Jackett installation one day started to give errors when trying to access 1337x. FlareSolverr operates as a local proxy server that uses real browser automation to bypass JavaScript based anti bot protection systems such as Cloudflare. About FlareSolverr FlareSolverr is a powerful proxy server designed to help applications bypass Cloudflare and other anti-bot protections automatically. ### B. HTML parsing & main-content extraction

Beneath every crawler in section 5 sits a parser, and beneath every "clean markdown" promise sits a boilerplate-removal algorithm. The parsing ladder: **BeautifulSoup** (ergonomic default; note the GitHub mirror below is dormant and archived — the project itself develops on Launchpad and the `beautifulsoup4` pip package remains current) → **lxml** (the C libxml2 binding bs4 uses for speed; also powers XPath everywhere) → **selectolax** (Lexbor engine binding, roughly an order of magnitude faster than lxml on large pages, CSS selectors only — the choice inside high-throughput crawlers). On the content side, the 2025–2026 benchmark literature (scrapinghub/article-extraction-benchmark; trafilatura's own evaluation suite; the arXiv WCXB multi-type benchmark; Thunderbit's 2026 fixtures where trafilatura leaked 1 of 17 annotated boilerplate units vs readability's 5) consistently crowns **trafilatura and mozilla/readability** (both already tabled in section 6) as the quality leaders, with **newspaper4k** (maintained fork of newspaper3k) the turnkey choice for news-article + metadata extraction, **jusText** an older heuristic now largely superseded by trafilatura, and **feedparser** the RSS/Atom counterpart that pairs with the feed-reader category of the main report.

### C. The Scrapy ecosystem

Section 5 tables Scrapy itself (★64.4k, pushed the day of this check). What deserves the deep dive is its surround: **parsel** is Scrapy's selector engine (XPath + CSS over lxml), usable standalone and quietly one of the most-installed parsing libraries in Python; **scrapy-playwright** is the now-standard hybrid — Scrapy keeps scheduling, deduplication and pipelines while JavaScript pages route through Playwright (current guidance covers scrapy-playwright 0.0.40+ on Scrapy 2.11+, with 2026 tutorials tracking Scrapy 2.18); **scrapy-redis** adds Redis-based scheduling/dupefilters for distributed crawls. This trio is the concrete answer to "why not just use the LLM-native crawlers": at scale, deterministic orchestration is free and LLM calls are not — the 2026 pattern is classic Scrapy for the crawl, LLMs only at the extraction edge.

### D. PDF & data foundations

The Python PDF triangle per the 2026 comparison literature: **pypdf** (pure Python, the current name of PyPDF2 — merge/split/rotate and basic text; zero table extraction) — **pdfminer.six** (the community-maintained pure-Python layout engine; the most stable library in the benchmarks, and the foundation pdfplumber builds its table introspection on, at the cost of speed and occasional multi-column reading-order failures noted in third-party benchmarks) — **PyMuPDF** (fastest and richest, AGPL-3.0 caveat for redistribution; both already tabled in section 6). Production pipelines typically pair pdfplumber (tables) with PyMuPDF (speed/rendering) and keep pypdf for page surgery. On the data side: **numpy** needs no introduction; **Apache Arrow** is the columnar interchange layer that lets polars, DuckDB, pandas and PyMuPDF-adjacent tooling interoperate zero-copy — and pandas 3.0 (PyArrow-backed strings, copy-on-write, expression improvements) has narrowed the gap that drove the polars migration, while polars retains 3–11× (up to 15× on grouped workloads in third-party benchmarks) leads on large lazy/streaming jobs. Two canonical-off-GitHub notes for completeness: **openpyxl** develops on Heptapod (Mercurial; the GitHub mirrors are ★74 forks), and SheetJS already carries that flag in section 7's table.

# Codebase Teardown — Tools for Deeply Analyzing and Understanding a Repository (2026-09)

**Scope.** The user's goal: *deeply analyze a codebase / repo project, understand its inner workings, perform a full teardown.* This report maps every layer of that job: AI-era repo comprehension and knowledge graphs, code search & navigation engines, static analysis and security teardown, architecture/dependency visualization, git-history forensics, size/complexity/dead-code metrics, dependency & supply-chain analysis, and runtime/dynamic analysis — then closes with a recommended teardown workflow that chains the layers together.

**Companions:** `oss-categories-report-2026-09.md` (65-category main report), `browser-android-scraping-deep-dive-2026-09.md` (scraping/extraction deep dive + classics addendum), `kb-distillation-tools-2026-09.md` (the context-pack tools repomix / gitingest / onefilellm / PocketFlow-Tutorial-Codebase-Knowledge / context7 are tabled there and cross-referenced here rather than repeated).

**Method.** Candidate discovery via the source listings (385-video showcase corpus + Product Hunt viewer) plus the research toolkit's free DDG engine across 10 query angles (large-codebase tooling roundups, DeepWiki alternatives, CPG/SAST comparisons, dependency-graph tools, git-analytics, SBOM tooling, SLOC counters, self-hosted code search, call-graph generators, MCP code-intelligence). **Every repo was health-verified via `gh api` on 2026-09-22** ($0 toolkit spend). Rows marked ＋ are web-researched; unmarked rows also appeared in the source listings. Several repos had been renamed or moved by check time — hound (now `hound-search/hound`), GritQL (now under Biome as `biomejs/gritql`), SCIP (spun out of Sourcegraph as `scip-code/scip`), git-quick-stats and cve-bin-tool (moved to their own org / OpenSSF), and OWASP DependencyCheck (from `jeremylong` to its own org) — tables show canonical slugs.

---

## 1. AI-era repo comprehension & knowledge graphs (the 2026 wave)

This is the layer that changed most, and it is enormous. The flagship is **Graphify** (★120k, pushed this week): it turns a repo — source, docs, SQL schemas, configs, even PDFs — into a queryable knowledge graph using local deterministic AST parsing with "every edge explained, no vector store," installed as a `/graphify` skill for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and Gemini CLI. **Understand-Anything** (★83.7k) delivers the same shape as an interactive knowledge graph you can search and question from inside AI editors. **aider** (★49.1k) matters here less as a coding tool than for its **repo-map** — the tree-sitter + PageRank context-ranking technique that most of this layer descends from. **codebase-memory-mcp** (★44.1k, listings-sourced) gives coding agents persistent structural memory over a repo; **deepwiki-open** (★18k, listings) is the OSS DeepWiki that generates an interactive RAG wiki from any GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket URL, with the .NET-based **OpenDeepWiki** as its main sibling. The tail (code-graph-rag, CodePrism, code-intelligence-mcp's 37 tree-sitter tools over a SQLite knowledge graph, RepoMapper) packs the same contract into MCP servers. **code2prompt / files-to-prompt** are the minimal packers that feed any of the above to a plain LLM. One cautionary row: **bloop** — the 2023-era AI code-search darling — is archived (last push 2024-12); third-party reporting notes it shut down in April 2026 with its domain parked, and Greptile pivoted from codebase Q&A to code review. The lesson the table encodes: this layer is young and consolidating fast — prefer the actively-pushed top of the table for anything load-bearing.

## 2. Code search & navigation engines

Before you can analyze code you have to find it, and at teardown scale `grep` dies. **ripgrep** (★68.5k) is the universal default — every AI coding agent shells out to it. **tree-sitter** (★27k) is not a search tool but the parser underneath half this document; **ast-grep** (★16k) and **gritql** (★4.6k, now maintained under the Biome org) put structural, AST-level search and codemods on top of it — "find all calls of X, not strings matching X." **universal-ctags** (★7.3k) is the classic offline symbol index; **codequery** wraps ctags+graphviz into a SQL-like query DB. For org-scale self-hosted search the ladder is **Hound** (simplest, ★5.9k) → **zoekt** (★1.9k, the trigram engine Sourcegraph was built on; indexed 31k Kubernetes files in ~6s in a 2026 test) → **OpenGrok** (★5k, the veteran full cross-reference server). **livegrep** (★2.2k) is the regex-in-browser alternative. **ripwire** (★2.3k, Red Hat ET) is the 2026 AI-context spin on the pattern — a zero-dependency C++ CLI + MCP server that curates grep results for coding agents. **scip** (★811) is the code-intelligence protocol/precise-index format — notable less for direct use than for what it signals: Sourcegraph closed its main monorepo (the `sourcegraph/sourcegraph` repo now 404s), and the OSS code-intelligence assets live on in this spun-out project.

## 3. Static analysis & security teardown

The deep-analysis backbone, where "teardown" means proving things about code rather than summarizing it. **CodeQL** (★10.1k) treats code as a queryable relational database — the deepest question-asking tool available, free for OSS research, and the engine behind GitHub code scanning. **Semgrep** (★16.7k, listings-sourced) is the speed king: pattern rules in YAML, seconds per repo, the pragmatic default for CI. **Joern** (★3.5k) generates **code property graphs** from C/C++, JVM bytecode and binaries — the security-research standard for vulnerability hunting in unfamiliar codebases, i.e. literal teardowns. **Infer** (Meta, ★15.7k) adds interprocedural bug finding for Java/C/C++/Objective-C. **SonarQube** (★11k public mirror) is the quality-gate platform: complexity, duplication and maintainability dashboards over the whole repo. The 2026 comparison literature positions these as complements, not competitors — Semgrep for speed and custom rules, CodeQL for semantic depth, Joern for hostile/unfamiliar code, SonarQube for the org-level scorecard.

## 4. Architecture, dependency graphs & visualization

Turning "I've read the code" into "I can see the shape." Per-ecosystem dependency mappers are the workhorses: **madge** (★10.2k, JS/TS module graphs + circular-dependency detection), **dependency-cruiser** (★7.2k, adds enforceable rules — orphans, unlisted deps, forbidden layers), **pydeps** (Python) and **pipdeptree** (★3k, the tree view). **Doxygen** (★6.6k) remains the reference documentation generator with call/caller graphs via Graphviz — unglamorous and still unmatched for C/C++ teardowns. **likec4** (★5.7k, listings-sourced ×2) is the 2026 diagrams-as-code pick for architecture. **CodeCharta** (★535) visualizes a codebase as an interactive 3D city where mountains are complexity — pairs beautifully with §5's hotspot metrics. Two archived legends close the section and merit prose, not just flags: **Sourcetrail** (★16.5k, archived 2021) was the interactive C++/Java/Python source explorer everyone still misses — its spiritual successors are the §1 knowledge-graph tools; **Structurizr CLI** (archived 2026-02) was Simon Brown's architecture-tooling bridge (the C4-model methodology lives on in likec4). CodeSee — a 2021-era "code map for onboarding" startup — is gone entirely; only a ★10 GitHub Action survives.

## 5. Git history forensics — churn, hotspots & evolution

The teardown question static tools can't answer: *why is the code like this, and which parts are risky?* **code-maat** (★2.6k) is Adam Tornhill's mining-tool for exactly that — churn analysis, hotspots (complexity × change frequency), knowledge concentration; CodeScene is its commercial productization. **git-quick-stats** (★7k, moved to its own org) is the fast daily-driver for contributor/commit stats. **git-history** (★13.7k) gives instant per-file evolution browsing in the browser. **Gource** (★13.1k) animates the repo's history as a growing tree — genuinely useful for spotting which subsystems absorbed the effort. **git-of-theseus** (★3k, ⚠stale) tracks cohort survival — the famous "half-life of code" analysis; **gitstats** (★1.7k, ⚠stale) is the classic HTML report generator; **hercules** (⚠src-d dissolved, engine still works) does deep branch/churn analysis in Go. The staleness flags here are mostly "finished software" rather than abandonment — churn math has not changed — but for new integrations prefer git-quick-stats + code-maat.

## 6. Size, complexity & dead-code metrics

The quantitative first pass of any teardown. Counters first: **cloc** (★23.6k) is the classic; **tokei** (★14.9k, Rust) and **scc** (★8.8k, Go) are the fast modern replacements, and scc adds per-language complexity estimates plus **COCOMO/LOCOMO project-cost estimation** — "this repo represents ~N person-years" is the single most illuminating line of a teardown intro. Then quality: **lizard** (★2.5k) measures cyclomatic complexity and NLOC across 40+ languages from one binary; **radon** (⚠slower cadence) is the Python-specific equivalent; **jscpd** (★6.3k) finds copy-paste duplication across 150+ languages. Dead code — the teardown's negative space: **vulture** (★4.8k) finds unused Python code, **knip** (★12.3k) is the 2026 standard for unused JS/TS exports, files and dependencies. The listings contribute **codex-complexity-optimizer** (★899), an agent-era wrapper that refactors complexity hotspots.

## 7. Dependency & supply-chain teardown

A modern repo is mostly other people's code — the teardown must cover the transitive dependency tree. **Trivy** (★38k, listings-sourced ×2) is the all-in-one: SBOM generation + vulnerability + secret + misconfiguration scanning of repos, images and filesystems. The 2026 consensus stack per the comparison literature: **syft** (★9.6k) to generate the SBOM → **grype** (★12.9k) to scan it (same Anchore ecosystem), or osv-scanner (★11.1k, listings) against Google's OSV database for the vulnerability-only pass. **ScanCode Toolkit** (★2.6k) is the license-compliance engine — which of your 800 transitive deps are GPL. **ORT** (★2.1k) is the heavyweight FOSS-policy automation suite (SBOM + license + vulnerability + attribution reports), and **Dependency-Track** (★4.2k) is the OWASP platform that continuously monitors SBOMs rather than scanning once. **cve-bin-tool** (now under OpenSSF) scans binaries for known CVEs. One org-move the verification caught: **OWASP DependencyCheck** relocated from the personal `jeremylong` repo (archived 2025-09) to its own org — the project is alive and pushed the day of this check; link the canonical `dependency-check/DependencyCheck`, not the archived original.

## 8. Runtime & dynamic analysis

When the code can be executed, the teardown graduates from inference to observation. **py-spy** (★15.5k) samples running Python processes without touching a line of code or restarting anything — find what the program actually spends time on. **FlameGraph** (★19.8k) is Brendan Gregg's canonical stack-visualizer that every profiler output can be folded into. **rr** (★10.7k) is the record-and-replay deterministic debugger — record a failing execution once, then walk it backwards and forwards in gdb; for C/C++ teardowns of crashes this is transformative. **pyinstrument** (★8k) is the low-overhead statistical Python profiler with honest call-tree output. **AppMap** records execution traces and renders them as interaction diagrams (the `appmap-js` monorepo is modest; the per-language agents live in the `getappmap` org). Rule of thumb: static layers (§1–§7) for *how it is built*, this layer for *how it actually behaves*.

## 9. A recommended full-teardown workflow

Chaining the layers into one repeatable pass over an unfamiliar repo, cheapest first:

1. **Inventory (minutes).** `scc` for languages, LOC, complexity and COCOMO person-year estimate; `cloc`/`tokei` to cross-check. One command, and you already know the size of what you're dealing with.
2. **AI comprehension pass (minutes–hours).** `graphify` (or Understand-Anything) to build the knowledge graph, or `deepwiki-open` for a wiki from the repo URL; feed `repomix`/`code2prompt` packs to your coding agent for Q&A. Use it to form hypotheses, not conclusions.
3. **Structure (an hour).** `madge`/`dependency-cruiser` (JS/TS), `pydeps`/`pipdeptree` (Python) for the dependency shape; `ast-grep` for structural queries; `doxygen` call graphs for C/C++; sketch the architecture in `likec4`.
4. **History (an hour).** `git-quick-stats` for contributor/commit shape, `code-maat` for churn hotspots, `Gource` for where the effort went, `git-history` for per-file archaeology. Hotspots tell you where to read deeply.
5. **Quality & security (hours).** `lizard`/`radon` complexity maps, `jscpd` duplication, `knip`/`vulture` dead code, then `semgrep` (fast pass) and `CodeQL` or `joern` (deep pass) for vulnerability classes. `CodeCharta` to see it all as a 3D city.
6. **Supply chain (an hour).** `syft` SBOM → `grype`/`trivy` CVEs, `scancode` license audit, `Dependency-Track` if this becomes recurring.
7. **Runtime (when runnable).** `py-spy`/`pyinstrument` profiling, `FlameGraph` visualization, `rr` for crash forensics, AppMap for interaction maps.

Static layers first, runtime last, AI comprehension woven through steps 2–5 — the agents are excellent at step 5's "explain this hotspot" once steps 1–4 have told them where to look.

# Infinite-Canvas FOSS Tools — Engines, Whiteboards, Node Editors and AI Canvases (2026-09)

**Scope.** Everything with a pan-and-zoom, unbounded 2D surface, in four layers: the engines and SDKs you embed, the end-user whiteboard apps, the node-based editors, and the 2026 wave of AI canvases where agents and generation live on the board. Fixed-page editors, desktop mind-map classics without a canvas surface, and proprietary canvases (Miro, FigJam, Flora, Krea, 8frame, Storyflow) are excluded. Obsidian's built-in Canvas is excluded because Obsidian is not open source — though an OSS plugin below covers that need. Verified as of 2026-09-22.

**Companions:** `oss-categories-report-2026-09.md` (65-category main report) · `uiux-design-prototyping-tools-2026-09.md` (design & prototyping deep dive) · `ui-component-libraries-2026-09.md` · `browser-android-scraping-deep-dive-2026-09.md` · `kb-distillation-tools-2026-09.md` · `codebase-teardown-tools-2026-09.md`.

**The 2026 landscape.** Two facts anchor the year. First, the two most-starred projects anywhere near this space are both canvases: Excalidraw at ★133k and ComfyUI at ★134k — one a hand-drawn whiteboard, the other a node-graph diffusion tool. The canvas is not a niche UI paradigm; it is where open source's biggest audiences live. Second, the GitHub `infinite-canvas` topic in 2026 is dominated not by drawing tools but by *agent workspaces* — projects describing themselves as infinite canvases for Claude Code, Codex, terminals, tasks and notes. When one human now supervises many parallel AI agents, the spatial canvas became the management interface: §E tables the tools built on exactly that premise.

The counter-thread is licensing. The most famous canvas SDK — tldraw — is no longer FOSS: source-available under its own license, free with a watermark in development, paid for production beyond small-business thresholds (SDK 4.0 is current). AFFiNE adopted split per-directory licensing, hero8152's canvas registers non-standard, and several young AI-canvas repos ship no license file at all. Against that, a MIT counter-wave: Excalidraw, Konva (standard MIT grant behind a confusing GitHub label), Fabric.js — and 2026's Quickdraw, an explicitly MIT open-source tldraw alternative benchmarking itself at a twentieth of the weight. Meanwhile the engines are quietly reorganizing: mxGraph died in 2020 and maxGraph carries its lineage; litegraph.js went quiet in 2024 and the Comfy-Org fork is the live branch.

**Method.** Candidate discovery from the GitHub `infinite-canvas` topic and gh repository search, the source listings corpus (385-video showcase + Product Hunt viewer), and 17 research-toolkit free-engine searches (DDG ladder, discovery class) across landscape, engine, node-editor, mind-map, AI-canvas and licensing angles. **Every tabled repo was health-verified via `gh api` on 2026-09-22** ($0 toolkit spend). Rows marked ＋ are web-researched; unmarked rows also appeared in the source listings. Verification resolved several identities: ComfyUI now lives at `Comfy-Org/ComfyUI` (moved from comfyanonymous), Quickdraw at `quickdrawjs/quickdraw`, TermCanvas at `blueberrycongee/termcanvas`, Dim0 at `vcmf/dim0`, DeepNotes at `DeepNotesApp/DeepNotes`, and the mxGraph successor at `maxGraph/maxGraph`. One candidate was dropped: the web mind-map project simple-mind-map, whose repository 404s at check time.

---

## A. Infinite-canvas engines & SDKs

The build-your-own layer. **tldraw** (★50k) is the category's polish leader and its licensing cautionary tale — source-available, watermark in development, paid for production. **Excalidraw** (★133k) is the MIT counterweight and the most-starred canvas project anywhere, as both an app and an embeddable React package. **Konva** and **Fabric.js** are the scene-graph and object-model veterans for custom drawing surfaces, **Quickdraw** (2026) is the new MIT challenger marketing itself as the open tldraw alternative at a claimed twentieth of the weight, **BlockSuite** is the only framework fusing block documents with an edgeless canvas in one data model (it powers §B's AFFiNE), and **maxGraph** carries the mxGraph lineage that draw.io was built on.

## C. Node-based & diagram editors

Boxes-and-wires canvases are their own engineering problem, and this layer has the most structural churn. **xyflow** (★38k; React Flow + Svelte Flow) is the default choice, with a paid Pro examples tier funding the MIT core. **Rete.js** adds the execution engine that actually runs the graph; **Drawflow** is the minimal vanilla option (⚠ frozen since 2024). The litegraph.js pair tells a succession story: the original — the canvas under ComfyUI's first frontend — went quiet in 2024, and the Comfy-Org fork is the live branch. **JointJS** (MPL-2.0 core plus commercial tier) anchors diagramming toolkits, and **ComfyUI** itself (★134k) is the largest deployment of a node canvas anywhere in FOSS.

## D. Mind-map & knowledge canvases

The knowledge layer. **markmap** renders markdown as an interactive, collapsible tree — the canvas as a derived view of files you already own, no editor required. The **Obsidian Excalidraw plugin** puts a live Excalidraw board inside Obsidian, where notes, PDFs and images become canvas elements — effectively the open-source stand-in for Obsidian's own non-OSS Canvas. **DeepNotes** is the end-to-end-encrypted bet on fractal page-within-page canvases. Honest note: the dedicated mind-map-canvas category thinned in 2026 — Freeplane and friends remain desktop classics without web canvases, and one prominent web mind-map project (simple-mind-map) saw its repository vanish between discovery and verification.

## E. AI-native agent & creation canvases

The 2026 wave, in two clusters. First, the Chinese-community AI creation workbenches: **basketikun's Infinite Canvas** (★6.9k, the breakout), **hero8152's** ComfyUI-connected variant and **tigerowo's** director-console take — OpenAI-compatible generation wired directly into spatial boards. Second, the agent-operations canvases: **TermCanvas** puts Claude Code, Codex and terminal tiles on one zoomable surface with per-tile status dots and session replay, while **Dim0** makes the board itself the agent's shared context. Between the clusters sit the Excalidraw bridges — **Excalidraw MCP**, the **diagram skill** and **Smart Excalidraw** — which let coding agents emit canvas-native artifacts instead of flat images, plus fal's **Infinite Kanvas** (⚠ quiet for a year). Stars here are small because the category is weeks to months old, not because the idea failed.

The AI layer is board-aware — notes, mini-apps and agents act on what is on the canvas, across eight switchable models — and everything is multiplayer, self-hostable and MIT-licensed, with the project positioning itself squarely against the Notion-plus-Miro-plus-Excalidraw stack. It is early: stars are in the low hundreds and the pitch outruns the polish. But it is the clearest expression of where the agent-canvas category is heading — the board as shared context that both humans and models read and write — and it was pushed the day of this check. |


---

## Recommendations by intent

- **Embed a whiteboard, zero license anxiety.** **Excalidraw**'s React package first; **Quickdraw** if you need React Native or a smaller core and accept a young project; **tldraw** only if you accept source-available terms for its polish.
- **Build a node-based UI.** **React Flow / Svelte Flow** (xyflow) by default; **Rete.js** when the graph must execute, not just display; **Drawflow** for minimal vanilla needs, minding the 2024 freeze; **litegraph.js via the Comfy-Org fork** for widget-heavy visual programming.
- **Diagramming application or embed.** **maxGraph** to inherit the mxGraph lineage cleanly, **JointJS** for a supported commercial-backed option, or simply ship **draw.io** today.
- **Personal or team knowledge canvas.** **AFFiNE** for teams wanting docs+canvas in one; **SiYuan** or **Logseq** for local-first PKM; **DeepNotes** when end-to-end encryption is the requirement; Obsidian users should live in the **Excalidraw plugin**.
- **Supervising AI agents.** **TermCanvas** for terminals and coding agents with worktree hierarchies; **Dim0** for a collaborative board where the AI reads everything.
- **AI image/video creation canvas.** **basketikun's Infinite Canvas** standalone, **hero8152's** when generation should run through your own ComfyUI install.
- **Native handwriting.** **Rnote** — the Rust canvas for stylus-first note-taking.

# Distilling Video Tutorials & Ebooks into LLM-Friendly Knowledge Bases — Tool Landscape

**Reference point:** `virgiliojr94/book-to-skill` (★32.0k, MIT, Python, pushed 2026-09-18) — the user's example tool. It converts technical books (PDF/EPUB/DOCX/MD/HTML/RTF/MOBI) into an **Agent Skill**: a `SKILL.md` index plus per-chapter distilled files (named frameworks, decision rules, anti-patterns — "structure, not a summary") that Claude Code, Copilot CLI, Amp, Hermes Agent, or OpenClaw **loads on demand**. Its measured payoff: **24×–51× fewer tokens** than dumping the book into context to answer one question. That pattern — *distill → structure → progressive disclosure* — is the organizing idea of this whole landscape.

**Scope.** The user's inputs are **programming video tutorials and ebooks**; the destination is a **knowledge base for coding agents**. This report maps every layer of that pipeline: direct book-to-skill analogs, video→transcript→skill/notes distillation, the NotebookLM route, self-hosted second-brain/KB platforms that serve agents, and the adjacent codebase→context-pack tools. Candidate discovery via GitHub search + the research toolkit's free DDG engine; **every repo below was health-verified via `gh api` on 2026-09-22** ($0 toolkit spend; Tavily untouched). Rows marked ＋ are web-researched additions; unmarked "＋"-less rows with `listings (...)` also appeared in the source showcase listings of the companion reports.

**A sizing note before the tables.** The distillation layer is young (most repos < 12 months old, several in the ★1–10k take-off band), while the foundations it sits on are enormous and mature: yt-dlp (★192.9k) and whisper (★107k) move more mass than everything else here combined. The gap between those two facts is exactly where the interesting 2026 tooling lives.

---

## 1. Direct analogs — books & documents → Agent Skills

book-to-skill has already spawned a recognizable genre. The most important sibling for this user is **cangjie-skill** (仓颯, ★10.5k, MIT): it distills **books AND long-form videos AND podcasts** into executable Agent Skills — i.e. it covers both of the user's input types in one tool, which book-to-skill proper does not (it handles documents; video arrives via transcript files). Below that are smaller variations on the same contract: a Chinese-language book-to-skill re-implementation, a PDF→callable-skills converter, and a LingTai-oriented "loop engineering" distillation skill. Around the genre sits a marketplace ecosystem (skills.rest `book-distiller`, book2skills.com, mcpmarket's `book-to-skill-converter` and `video-knowledge-extractor` skills) — commercial or listing-page evidence of demand, not verified OSS, so cited here rather than tabled.

## 2. Video tutorials → transcripts → distilled knowledge

Video distillation decomposes into three stages, and the tooling is strongest at the ends.

**(a) Acquisition & transcription** — the foundation layer. yt-dlp (★192.9k, Unlicense) downloads any tutorial playlist; `youtube-transcript-api` (★8.4k) fetches official captions with no API key; yt2doc and yt-whisper wrap the download→transcribe→clean step. For local video files or uncaptioned tutorials, the whisper family applies (openai/whisper ★107k, SYSTRAN/faster-whisper ★25k — 3–4× faster, same accuracy — and m-bain/whisperX ★23.6k with word-level timestamps; all three health-verified in the companion report).

**(b) Distillation into agent-usable knowledge** — the young, fast-moving layer. claude-video (★17.5k) is the flagship: a Claude skill where `/watch` downloads a video, extracts frames, transcribes, and hands everything to the agent — multimodal, which matters for programming tutorials where the code is on screen, not in the audio. claude-real-video (★2.2k) refines the same idea with scene-aware deduplicated frames. ZeroPointRepo/youtube-skills (★901) gives agents transcript search/browse primitives; the smaller entries (youtube-digest-skill, claude-youtube-skill, skill-pack's video-to-note, KIRVO's video-to-notes with Notion/Obsidian export) each package one distillation contract.

**(c) Research-grade video understanding** — VideoAgent (HKUDS, EMNLP 2026) represents the agentic-research direction; overkill for a personal KB, included for completeness.

## 3. The NotebookLM route

Google NotebookLM is the mainstream answer to "videos + PDFs → structured study knowledge", and the OSS ecosystem clusters around it in two ways: **API wrappers/skills** that let coding agents drive your notebooks (notebooklm-py ★19.4k — unofficial Python API exposing features the web UI doesn't; qiaomu's anything-to-notebooklm ★6.1k — YouTube/PDF/Markdown in, podcasts/mind-maps/quizzes out), and **self-hosted reimplementations** (open-notebook ★39.4k, SurfSense ★16.2k air-gapped, notebookllama ★2k). ⚠ Both PleasePrompto projects (notebooklm-skill ★7.8k, notebooklm-mcp ★3.4k) were **archived on the same day, 2026-09-10** — a caution signal for anything building on unofficial NotebookLM access; the actively-pushed path today is notebooklm-py.

## 4. Second-brain / KB platforms that serve coding agents

The serving layer: where the distilled markdown lives and how agents query it. Two architectural camps. **Markdown-native** (the Karpathy "LLM wiki" pattern): claude-obsidian (★15.1k) drops any source into a self-organizing Obsidian graph of plain Markdown your agent reads and links; obsidian-second-brain (★4.6k) gives seven CLI agents persistent vault memory with hybrid semantic search; kepano/obsidian-skills (★48.7k, from Obsidian's CEO) teaches agents the Obsidian CLI and open formats; karpathy/reader3 (★3.9k) is the minimal "read books with LLMs" reference. **Server-native RAG**: anything-llm (★66.3k, workspaces with documents + YouTube transcript ingestion), khoj (★37.5k second brain), quivr (★39.5k). For coding agents specifically, the markdown-native camp is the better fit — the files double as agent-readable context with zero serving infrastructure, and basic-memory (★4.0k) bridges the two worlds as an MCP memory server over markdown.

## 6. Recommended stacks for the user's exact case

Three viable assemblies, from lightest to heaviest:

1. **CLI-native (recommended start).** `yt-dlp` (or `youtube-transcript-api` for captioned videos) → `faster-whisper`/`whisperX` for uncaptioned/local files → **cangjie-skill** for videos *and* ebooks (or **book-to-skill** for the ebook half) → resulting `skills/` folder dropped into `.claude/skills` (or `.openclaw/skills`). Everything is plain markdown files; every agent in the report's companion docs can read them; zero serving infra. For code-on-screen tutorials, add **claude-video**'s frame extraction.
2. **Obsidian-centered.** Same distillation, but land the output in an Obsidian vault; serve it with **obsidian-skills** (agent uses the vault via CLI) + **claude-obsidian** (auto-links and files new sources as you add them). Best when the KB is also for human study — the wiki graph is browsable and the same files feed the agents.
3. **RAG-server.** Land transcripts and extracted book text in **anything-llm** (native YouTube-transcript ingestion) or **open-notebook**, query via API/MCP. Best when the corpus outgrows on-demand skill loading or multiple non-CLI consumers need it.

**What to avoid:** the archived PleasePrompto NotebookLM pair (dead as of 2026-09-10); ★<200 experiments for anything load-bearing.

# Free & Open-Source Tools Across 65 Categories — Research Report

**Scope.** Extract every GitHub repo, free-to-use, and open-source software product from the two documents in `listings/` — `index.html` ("GitHub Repo Showcase": 7,268 repo entries distilled from 385 YouTube showcase videos across 39 channels) and `products_viewer_unified.html` (11,226 Product Hunt products, Jun–Sep 2026) — bucket them into the 65 requested categories, and recommend per category with the full source-table-row metadata. The two documents share **zero overlapping URLs**: they are disjoint sources (falsifiability check #1 passed). The URL intersection being exactly 0 was verified by script, not assumed.

**Method.**
1. Both embedded datasets were extracted programmatically (the HTML apps are self-contained; data lives in an embedded `const DATA` array and an embedded JSON island). 7,268 repo rows + 11,226 PH rows.
2. PH products were split by OSS signal: 751 with strong open-source/self-host signals (license/OSS/GitHub mentions) and 631 free-only were carried forward as candidates.
3. All ~19K rows were scored against weighted keyword rules per category (name ×3, topics/tags ×2, description ×1), then **manually curated**: the automated digest was reviewed category-by-category and obvious mis-buckets (e.g. tiptap under Unity editor automation, uv under backups) were removed, duplicates merged (same repo shown in multiple videos → keep max stars, count sources), and picks re-checked.
4. Every recommended repo was health-verified via `gh api repos/OWNER/REPO` on **2026-09-22** (stars, forks, license, archived, last push). The ★ column shows `listing→GH` when the listing number and today's number differ. Categories where the listings had thin or no coverage received clearly-marked **＋ web gap-fill** additions (canonical tools confirmed against 2026 comparison sources via the research toolkit's DDG engine).
5. Local README documentation (3,197 folders at the permitted `repo-showcase-studio/output/repos` path) was available for enrichment; no other file from that tree was consulted.

**Caveats.** Star counts in the listing document are as-of their capture dates and disagree with live GitHub for 299 of the recommended repos — the report shows both. `⚠archived` / `⚠stale` flags come from the live check. PH rows carry the viewer document's metadata (upvotes at capture, tags, months). "Free-to-use" PH products without an OSS signal were only included where the category had thin OSS coverage and are visible via their tags.

**As of 2026-09-22. Toolkit spend: $0 (all searches via the free DDG engine; Tavily allowance untouched this session).**

| **BugProof** | 9 | Productivity, Open Source, Developer Tools | June 2026 | no | Executable bugs, not bug reports | Executable bugs, not bug reports. BugProof captures a failing command — environment, arguments, exit status, output and the minimal inputs needed to reproduce it — into a portable .bug artifact that anyone can replay on their own machine: the bug reproduces by definition, because what is replayed is the recorded execution rather than prose steps a human must re-interpret. Billed as Git for bugs, artifacts are diffable, shareable and installable in about ten seconds, closing the it-works-on-my-machine gap between reporter and fixer. Because replays are deterministic, CI can run the artifact as a regression test once a fix lands, and a replay that stops failing marks the bug fixed for good. |

It's built for teams who want a CRM that actually keeps itself up to date without hallucinating customer facts, and for self-hosters who need to reconfigure without redeploying. It solves the problem of verifying whether a DNS record has propagated globally by querying each resolver directly in parallel — bypassing caches via EDNS0 with TCP fallback — and continuously re-polling until full propagation is reached. Round-robin DNS results sharing the same record are grouped into a single majority answer, with outliers flagged, and a propagation gauge shows what percentage of resolvers agree. Users get the anycast network's actual answering site (Quad9, Cloudflare, Google, OpenDNS, CleanBrowsing, Neustar) through their identification TXT queries, with the map dot moving to the real POP. Optional EDNS Client Subnet support lets users see how GeoDNS answers from different client network vantage points, and a TOML config file allows adding custom resolvers, forcing the map/globe view, or theming the UI. The tool targets sysadmins, DNS operators, and web developers debugging propagation issues, and is distributed via Homebrew, crates.io, the Arch AUR, Nix flakes, and prebuilt binaries. |

Agent Orchestrator (AO) is the open-source control plane for running many coding agents at once: dispatch tasks across a fleet of Claude Code/Codex-style workers, watch their sessions, and collect results — with an orchestrator agent acting as manager over the whole fleet, decomposing work and assigning it. The launch cites 9.5k+ GitHub stars and developers managing thousands of agents daily through AO, reflecting the 2026 shift from one assistant to parallel agent teams that need queuing, budgets and oversight. The project is open source, so the fleet-manager layer itself can be audited, extended and self-hosted alongside the agents it supervises. |

RiskKernel is an open-source, self-hosted runtime that wraps any agent with deterministic limits — per-run cost caps, loop detection, and wall-clock time budgets — plus a real kill switch that stops a runaway session on the spot, crash-resumable runs so a stopped agent continues cleanly, and human-approval gates where high-risk actions wait for sign-off. It exists because production agents loop, burn tokens, and ship consequences with no off switch; this is the off switch, as infrastructure rather than a prompt suggestion. Deterministic means the limits are enforced in code around the agent, not merely requested of the model. |

| **MCP Context Budget** | 5 | Open Source, Developer Tools, Artificial Intelligence | June 2026 | no | Measure and cap MCP context bloat before agents run | Measure and cap MCP context bloat before agents run. Every connected MCP server injects its full tool schemas — names, descriptions, parameter types, JSON Schemas — into the context at session start, and a handful of servers can quietly consume a large slice of your window before the first real message. This tool counts exactly that: per-server token cost of tool definitions and system prompt, visibility into which servers are worth their footprint, and caps that keep context bloat in check — fixing MCP's silent token tax at configuration time instead of mid-task. Capping bloated servers at configuration time beats discovering the problem mid-task with a truncated session. |

# UI Component Libraries — npm and Copy-Paste Kits for React/Next.js, Svelte and Flutter (2026-09)

**Scope.** Traditional (npm-installed) and copy-paste/registry component libraries, focused on the user's front-ends — React/Next.js, Svelte (5), and Flutter/Dart — plus the framework-agnostic Tailwind/HTML/Web-Component kits any of those stacks can consume, and the agent-side tooling that composes components programmatically. The **Frameworks** column states each library's targets and the **Type** column its distribution model. A companion deep dive, `uiux-design-prototyping-tools-2026-09.md`, covers the design/prototyping/generation tools; this report covers what your app is actually built from.

**The 2026 landscape.** The headline event: **the copy-paste model out-scaled the npm incumbents.** shadcn/ui — not a package but a CLI that puts component source code into your repository — reached ★124k, past Ant Design (★99.6k) and Material UI (★99.1k), every one of which is older and more fully featured. Its registry protocol became the ecosystem's distribution primitive (the May 2026 shadcn release added `include` and `validate` operations for safely consuming third-party registries), and the model jumped frameworks: shadcn-svelte for Svelte, flutter-shadcn-ui and forui for Flutter, daisyUI's plugin form for anything Tailwind. The npm side did not stand still: **headless primitives consolidated** — Radix's creators shipped Base UI under the MUI org, and shadcn/ui itself now generates against Base UI and React Aria in addition to Radix; Zag.js powers both Ark UI (React/Solid/Vue/Svelte) and Chakra v3. **Svelte 5 reached maturity** — bits-ui is the headless engine, shadcn-svelte moved under its author's org (huntabyte) and stayed active, while melt-ui's predecessor stalled (last push 2025-09). **Flutter caught the shadcn wave** (flutter-shadcn-ui renamed from shadcn_flutter, pushed this week) while the SDK itself began decoupling Material and Cupertino into separate packages. Consolidation of another kind: Origin UI was absorbed into Cal.com's design system as **Coss** (AGPL-3.0 — a license change worth noting). One exclusion for honesty: Aceternity UI ships no open-source repository — its components are free-to-copy from proprietary docs, so it is named here but not tabled.

**Method.** Candidates hand-curated from the source listings (385-video showcase corpus + Product Hunt viewer) plus research-toolkit free-engine searches across component-library landscape angles (DDG ladder, discovery class). **Every repo was health-verified via `gh api` on 2026-09-22** ($0 toolkit spend). Rows marked ＋ are web-researched; unmarked rows also appeared in the source listings.

## 2. Headless primitives — npm

The unstyled behavior layer that styled kits build on. **Radix Primitives** (★19.3k) is the incumbent; its creators now also ship **Base UI** under the MUI org, which shadcn/ui can target as an alternative primitive engine. **React Aria Components** (in the `adobe/react-spectrum` monorepo, ★15.9k) is Adobe's accessibility engine, both a library and the a11y substrate inside HeroUI. **Zag.js** is the framework-agnostic state-machine core, and **Ark UI** (★5.4k) packages it for React, Solid, Vue and — officially since 2025 — Svelte. On the Svelte side specifically: **bits-ui** (★3.6k) is the Svelte 5 headless engine (and shadcn-svelte's foundation) while **melt-ui** (★4.2k), the previous standard, has gone quiet (last push 2025-09) — the ecosystem's succession is visible in the push dates.

## 3. Copy-paste / registry kits (React/Next)

The distribution model that won 2026: source code lands in your repo, you own it. **shadcn/ui** (★124k) is the archetype — see the landscape intro for its May 2026 registry `include`/`validate` additions. Around it, a constellation of registries: **Magic UI** and **Motion Primitives** for animated components, **Animate UI** (⚠license reads non-standard, ⚠last push 2025-12) and **Animata** for motion patterns, **fancy** for micro-interactions, **Origin UI → Coss** (now Cal.com's AGPL design system), **dotUI** as a design-system builder, and **Kibo UI** as a composable shadcn-compatible registry. **Canvas UI** brings the same copy-paste model to Svelte 5 with canvas-rendered components. Every one of these installs via the shadcn CLI or a direct copy — there is no runtime dependency to lock you in.

Svelte 5 is a first-class citizen in 2026. **shadcn-svelte** (★9.1k, now under `huntabyte` — the bits-ui author's org) ports the full shadcn workflow to Svelte with its own CLI; **Skeleton** (★6.1k) is the Tailwind-based design toolkit that deliberately integrates headless engines (bits-ui among them); **Flowbite Svelte** ports the Flowbite component set; **Svelte Animations** brings Magic-UI/Aceternity-style animated components; **Ark UI** (§2) covers headless officially. **SvGrid** (★178, young) is the Svelte 5 data grid — headless engine plus drop-in render components. **gpuix-svelte** is the experimental edge: a custom Svelte renderer that compiles components to native GPUI (Zed's GPU-accelerated framework) windows with no webview — directly relevant to Tauri-style desktop ambitions. ## 5. Framework-agnostic kits (Tailwind plugins, HTML, Web Components)

Libraries no framework owns. **daisyUI** (★42.5k) is the Tailwind plugin that gives you component classes in pure CSS — it works in Svelte, React, or a static HTML file, and 2026's "best component library" debates routinely shortlist it. **Flowbite** (★9.4k) ships Tailwind component markup you copy; **Preline UI** does the same on Headless-UI-patterned HTML; **Oat** (★5.5k) is the radical minimal end — semantic HTML/CSS/JS in ~10KB with zero dependencies; **Phantom UI** distributes a single structure-aware skeleton-loader Web Component (built with Lit) that works in any framework. These kits matter most for the multi-platform stack: one Tailwind/HTML kit can serve a SvelteKit web app and a Tauri desktop shell from the same markup vocabulary.

It works by rendering the real component with transparent placeholder text, measuring every leaf element's position and size via `getBoundingClientRect`, and overlaying animated shimmer blocks at those exact coordinates while preserving container backgrounds and borders. Because it is a standards-based custom element, it integrates with React, Vue, Svelte, Angular, Solid, Qwik, HTMX, and plain HTML without framework-specific adapters. Installation options include npm, bun, pnpm, yarn, a CDN script tag, or a vendored standalone ES module (34 kB minified, 11.5 kB gzipped) for projects without registry access or `node_modules`, with TypeScript declarations that type-check under strict mode with no configuration. An optional `init` command auto-generates JSX type declarations for React, Solid, and Qwik and adds pre-hydration CSS for SSR frameworks like Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, Remix, and Qwik, while leaving the codebase untouched when skipped (no postinstall hook runs). |

## 6. Flutter (Dart) — pub.dev libraries

The baseline is the SDK itself: **Material and Cupertino widgets** — Material 3 is Flutter's default design language, and the Flutter team is actively decoupling Material/Cupertino from the core framework into separate packages (a live 2026 development covered in the companion report). Above it: **flutter-shadcn-ui** (★2.8k, ex shadcn_flutter, pushed this week) and **forui** (★2.4k, Duobase) bring the shadcn look to Dart; **fluent_ui** (★3.5k) and **macos_ui** (★2.1k) give Tauri-parallel platform fidelity for Windows and macOS desktop builds; **getwidget** (★4.8k, now under ionicfirebaseapp) is the large Material-component catalog. The pattern to notice: Flutter's 2026 story is the shadcn model arriving (design-system-first, copy-friendly) while the SDK itself gets more modular.

## 7. Agent-side component tooling

How coding agents consume the libraries above. **shadcn-ui-mcp-server** (★3k) exposes shadcn components and third-party registries to MCP clients, so an agent can browse, install, and compose components instead of hallucinating markup. **Tambo** is a generative-UI toolkit — React components designed to be rendered by LLMs at runtime with streaming state. **tweakcn** (cross-referenced from the companion report) closes the loop by letting agents (or humans) theme the whole shadcn stack through generated CSS variables. Together with the design skills in the companion report's §D, this is the 2026 answer to "how does the AI build UI that doesn't look generic."

## Recommendations by stack

- **React / Next.js.** Default to **shadcn/ui** on Base UI or Radix primitives + Tailwind, themed with **tweakcn**; supplement animated pieces from **Motion Primitives** or **Magic UI**. If you want an installed package instead: **Mantine** (DX) or **Material UI** (enterprise completeness, MUI X data grid). Dashboard-heavy: **Tremor**. Design-token governance: companion report §E.
- **Svelte 5.** **shadcn-svelte** (its own CLI, bits-ui inside) for the component vocabulary; **Skeleton** if you want a designed system with headless flexibility; **Ark UI** for pure headless needs; **daisyUI** for CSS-only components in plain markup; **gpuix-svelte** if you're chasing native-GPU rendering experiments. Avoid building new work on **melt-ui** — its successor path is bits-ui.
- **Flutter / Dart.** Start from SDK Material 3 (watch the Material/Cupertino decoupling), add **flutter-shadcn-ui** or **forui** for the shadcn aesthetic, **fluent_ui**/**macos_ui** when desktop fidelity matters, and catalog everything in **Widgetbook** (companion report §A).
- **Tauri.** The webview renders whatever the web stack ships: shadcn-svelte + daisyUI/Oat for a light, fast shell; **Canvas UI**/gpuix-svelte are the Svelte-native experiments aimed squarely at desktop rendering.

# UI/UX Design & Prototyping — FOSS Tools for SvelteKit, Flutter, Tauri and Beyond (2026-09)

**Scope.** Tools for UI/UX design, rapid wireframing and prototyping, visual editing over real code, and image/screenshot/wireframe-to-code generation — for a stack of SvelteKit/Svelte 5 web apps, Flutter/Dart multiplatform apps, and Tauri desktop apps. All frameworks are included (React/Next.js dominates this space and is represented throughout); the **Frameworks supported** column states each tool's reach. The report closes with stack-specific recommendations.

**Companions:** `oss-categories-report-2026-09.md` (65-category main report) · `ui-component-libraries-2026-09.md` (the component-library deep dive) · `browser-android-scraping-deep-dive-2026-09.md` · `kb-distillation-tools-2026-09.md` · `codebase-teardown-tools-2026-09.md`.

**The 2026 landscape.** Two shifts define the year. First, *AI-native generation arrived as the default way new UI gets drafted*: Figma itself shipped Make (prompt-to-design inside the canvas), Vercel's v0 generated a whole class of open-source imitators, and the self-hostable bolt.diy / screenshot-to-code lineage became standard equipment. Independent testing in 2026 (miromiro.app's screenshot-to-code accuracy benchmarks across v0, Cursor and friends) found these tools genuinely productive for first drafts while still needing an engineer's pass for design-system fidelity. Anthropic's Claude Design (April 2026) then packaged conversational design — prompt, on-canvas editing, design-system sync with Claude Code — as a product; §F covers the open-source tools that answer it. Second, *the canvas-first design tools consolidated rather than died*: Penpot reached ★60k as the self-hostable Figma alternative — a 2026-06 retrospective (it crossed 52k that June) credits self-hosting and open standards, and the W3C Design Tokens Community Group's exchange format reached stable adoption backed by Adobe, Figma and Tokens Studio — which is exactly where the two shifts meet: tokens are how an AI-generated UI inherits a real design system. The interesting middle ground — visual editors that operate *on your existing codebase* (Onlook, Plasmic) instead of exporting from a parallel canvas — is where open source now out-innovates the proprietary tools. The prediction this report set out to falsify — that AI-native design has displaced canvas-first tools as the dominant new-project category — holds for *generation*, but not for *design systems*, where canvas-plus-tokens remains the source of truth.

**Method.** Candidate discovery from the source listings (385-video showcase corpus + Product Hunt viewer), then research-toolkit free-engine searches across 16 landscape angles plus per-tool queries (DDG ladder, discovery class). **Every repo was health-verified via `gh api` on 2026-09-22** ($0 toolkit spend). Rows marked ＋ are web-researched; unmarked rows also appeared in the source listings. Verification resolved several moves: openv0 now lives at `nraiden/openv0` (stale since 2024), Ark UI at `chakra-ui/ark`, Tokens Studio at `tokens-studio/figma-plugin`, and getwidget at `ionicfirebaseapp/getwidget`. **Section F** was added by follow-up request: it establishes what Anthropic's Claude Design is (launched April 2026) and tables the six open-source tools built in its mold — converse, generate, edit visually, stay on-brand, round-trip to code — all gh-verified 2026-09-22.

---

## A. Design & prototyping platforms

The canvas layer. **Penpot** (★60k) is the anchor: open source, self-hostable, SVG-native (so designs stay web-standards-clean), with W3C DTCG design-token support that pipes directly into the §E tooling. **OpenPencil** (★8.6k, pushed this week) is the 2026 AI-native challenger — a Tauri+Vue+Skia editor with built-in AI that opens .fig files and turns prompts into prototypes. **Quant-UX** adds the layer designers keep asking Figma for: integrated usability testing and analytics on interactive prototypes. **Excalidraw** (★133k — the most-starred repo in this report) and **tldraw** (★50k) are the infinite-canvas engines — hand-drawn wireframing and an embeddable React SDK respectively — and **Wireflow** covers user-flow mapping (⚠stale since 2024). Two structural picks: **Design OS** codifies the spec-before-code workflow that AI coding tools need to produce non-generic output, and **Widgetbook** is the Storybook-style workbench where a Flutter design system actually gets reviewed. Note for proprietary context: Figma shipped its own Make (prompt-to-design) in this cycle — the open answers are §C's generators plus Penpot's token pipeline.

## C. Screenshot / image / wireframe → code

The generation layer. **screenshot-to-code** (abi) is the canonical reference — mockup, screenshot or Figma frame in, React/Vite/HTML out, fully local. **OpenUI** (W&B) adds conversational iteration and converts generated HTML to React, Svelte or Vue. **bolt.diy** (★20k) is the self-hostable full-stack builder — 19+ LLM providers, WebContainers-based live preview, supports React/Next/Svelte/Vue and more. **cofounder** (★6.7k) is the 2026 continuation of openv0's idea: full-stack admin+app scaffolds from prompts. The napkins → **llamacoder** → **draw-a-ui** trio covers the "photo of a napkin sketch / hand-drawn wireframe" entry points (draw-a-ui ⚠stale since 2024), **ScreenCoder** handles video capture of UIs, and **ai-website-cloner-template** clones an existing site's look as a starting point. **dewhale** delivers v0-style prototypes as GitHub pull requests. Reality check from 2026 testing: these tools excel at *first drafts* and *cloning existing patterns*; design-system fidelity still comes from the §E token pipeline plus human refinement. React dominates output targets; **OpenUI's Svelte conversion and bolt.diy's multi-framework support are the exceptions that matter for a SvelteKit stack.**

## D. AI design intelligence & skills

The 2026-native layer: design knowledge packaged as agent skills and rulesets rather than applications. **taste-skill** (★89k — out-scaling nearly every component library in the companion report) teaches coding agents visual-taste heuristics for UI polish. **UI UX Pro Max** (★129.6k — this report's second-largest repo, behind only Excalidraw) generates complete design systems (personas, tokens, style guides) as agent-readable specs before code generation starts. **ui-skills** (from Motion Primitives' author) brings interaction-design refinement rules to agents, and **Uncodixfy** is a ruleset that constrains AI UI generation to quality standards. These are stack-agnostic by construction — the skill emits whatever framework the agent writes — and they compose: pair one with §C's generators and the generic-output problem largely dissolves. This category did not exist two years ago; it is the clearest evidence of the AI-native displacement claim.

## E. Design systems & tokens

The connective tissue between design and code, and the layer where 2026's W3C DTCG format stabilization mattered most. **Style Dictionary** (Amazon) is the build system: token JSON in, platform outputs out (CSS variables, Tailwind configs, iOS/Android/Compose, SCSS — anything scriptable). **Tokens Studio for Figma** is the design-side source of truth: define tokens in the canvas, sync to Git as JSON, review changes in pull requests. **Design Extract** (★4.1k) is the newest and most interesting — one command reverse-engineers a live website's complete design system into DTCG semantic/primitive/composite tokens, as a CLI, Chrome extension, MCP server and agent skill. For a SvelteKit+Flutter+Tauri stack this trio is the whole pipeline: extract or design the tokens once, transform to CSS variables for Svelte/Tailwind, Material theme data for Flutter, and shared Tauri theming.

## F. Claude Design–style conversational design tools

The reference point. Anthropic Labs launched **Claude Design** in April 2026 (claude.ai/design, research preview on paid plans): a conversational prompt-to-design workspace where Claude produces interactive prototypes, one-pagers, slides and decks that you refine by chatting *and* by direct on-canvas WYSIWYG editing. A June 2026 update added importable design systems — keeping output on-brand — plus PDF/PPTX export and desktop support, and the two-way `/design-sync` bridge with Claude Code (as of September 2026) connects canvas and repo in both directions: your codebase's real design system flows into the canvas, generated designs flow back as code. The workflow, in short: **converse → generate → edit visually → stay on-brand → round-trip to code.** The six tools tabled below were built explicitly in that mold; the facet-by-facet paragraph maps the remaining facets onto sections A–E.

The closest single match is **OpenDesign** (★97.6k, five months from launch — the fastest-growing new entrant in this report): a local-first desktop app whose design engine is the coding agent you already run, with its DESIGN.md design-system contracts playing the role of Claude Design's design-system import. **Open CoDesign** (★8k, MIT) is the lighter BYOK desktop take — prompt to prototype or slides with your own model key. **Dyad** (★21.6k) reproduces the converse-generate-iterate loop for full-stack apps rather than canvases. **Presenton** (★10.7k) covers the use case Anthropic itself calls one of Claude Design's most popular — decks and one-pagers — as a self-hosted generator with editable-PPTX output. **Huashu Design** (★24.4k) packages the workflow as a *skill*: twenty design philosophies and a five-dimensional review driving any coding agent to high-fidelity output. And the namesake **OpenPencil (ZSeven)** (★6k) adds concurrent agent teams and Design-as-Code on a live canvas — mind the name collision with §A's open-pencil/open-pencil.

Facet by facet, the rest of the workflow is already tabled elsewhere in this report: conversational generation with live preview is §C's **bolt.diy** and **OpenUI**; the canvas-native prompt-to-prototype loop is §A's **OpenPencil**; visual editing over real code — the `/design-sync` analog that lives inside the repo — is §B's **Onlook** (React) and **Plasmic**; on-brand grounding is §E's **Tokens Studio → Style Dictionary** pipeline plus §D's **ui-ux-pro-max-skill** and **taste-skill**. Honest gaps: no FOSS tool replicates the full two-way repo↔canvas sync end-to-end (OpenDesign comes structurally closest by making the repo's own agent the engine), and the polish ceiling depends on the model you point it at — Claude Design's edge is Anthropic's vision models, while every tool here is bring-your-own.

## Recommendations by stack

- **SvelteKit / Svelte 5.** Design in **Penpot** (or draft fast in **OpenPencil**), tokens via **Tokens Studio → Style Dictionary → CSS variables/Tailwind**. Generate first-draft UI with **OpenUI** (Svelte conversion) or **bolt.diy** (Svelte templates), refine with **taste-skill** in your agent, then adopt components from the companion report's Svelte section (shadcn-svelte, Skeleton, bits-ui). Visual editing over Svelte codebases is the one gap with no strong OSS answer today — Onlook/Plasmic are React-only.
- **Flutter / Dart.** **Widgetbook** as the component workbench; Material 3 + Cupertino from the SDK (being decoupled into separate packages — a live 2026 Flutter development); platform shells from **fluent_ui** (Windows) and **macos_ui** (macOS); shadcn-look components from **flutter-shadcn-ui** or **forui**. **Design Extract** → Material `ThemeData` bridges an existing brand into Flutter without a designer.
- **Tauri desktop.** The webview is a full browser, so every Tailwind/tokens tool above applies directly; **tweakcn** themes and **GrapesJS** output embed cleanly; OpenPencil itself is built with Tauri (existence proof for the stack). Pair with the component libraries in the companion report's framework-agnostic section.
